Drawing networks

Source: vignettes/articles/drawing-networks.qmd

This guide covers the drawing of a network. A network has no natural position on a page: it is a set of nodes and of ties, and the figure we see depends on coordinates that something has to compute. This is the job of a layout, and the choice of the layout shapes what the reader sees. The guide starts from the bibliographic coupling network of the explanations of the 1970s stagflation built in the first guide, whose clusters were detected in the second one.

library(networkflow)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

nodes <- subset(Nodes_stagflation, source_type == "Stagflation")
network <- build_network(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  method = "similarity",
  edges_threshold = 2,
  filter_components = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
network <- add_clusters(
  network,
  clustering_method = "leiden",
  objective_function = "modularity",
  resolution = 1,
  seed = 123,
  verbose = FALSE
)
network <- name_clusters(
  network,
  method = "tf-idf",
  cluster_id = "cluster_leiden",
  text_columns = "source_title",
  nb_terms_label = 3,
  clean_word_method = "lemmatize"
)

We keep the main component of a network with a threshold of two shared references (filter_components = TRUE): some layouts push the small, disconnected components far away from the rest, and the main component is the one we want to read.

What a layout does

A layout is a function that gives each node i a position p_i \in \mathbb{R}^2. Most layouts used in bibliometrics are force-directed: they treat the network as a physical system, in which tied nodes attract each other and all nodes repel each other, and look for positions where the forces balance. The clusters of a network, which are dense regions, then appear as groups of nodes close to each other.

layout_networks() computes the coordinates and adds them to the node table, in columns x and y. The layouts of igraph and graphlayouts are available through ggraph::create_layout(); "forceatlas2" and "umap" are added by networkflow.

Two cautions apply to all of them. First, layouts are stochastic (they start from random positions) and sensitive to their starting point: another seed gives another, equally valid picture, so set a seed before calling the function to reproduce a figure. Second, distances in the picture are only roughly interpretable. Two clusters drawn side by side are more tied than two clusters at opposite ends, but distances should not be measured, and a layout is a compromise between many constraints.

Force-directed layouts

Fruchterman-Reingold

Fruchterman-Reingold ("fr") is the default choice of networkflow (Fruchterman and Reingold 1991). With d the distance between two nodes and k an ideal distance, every pair of nodes repels with a force k^2/d, and every pair of tied nodes attracts with a force d^2/k, multiplied by the weight of the tie in igraph: heavier edges pull nodes closer.

set.seed(1)
laid_out <- layout_networks(network, node_id = "source_id", layout = "fr")
head(as_tibble(laid_out, active = "nodes")[c("source_id", "cluster_leiden", "x", "y")])
# A tibble: 6 × 4
  source_id cluster_leiden       x     y
  <chr>     <chr>            <dbl> <dbl>
1 96284971  04             -5.02   -3.05
2 214927    05             -8.54    3.65
3 2207578   05             -2.93    5.91
4 10729971  05             -6.48    1.68
5 95575910  03             -0.0142  1.73
6 105203318 03              1.66    1.71

Kamada-Kawai, and a trap with weights

Kamada-Kawai ("kk") takes the opposite approach (Kamada and Kawai 1989): it places the nodes so that their geometric distances reproduce their graph distances, as if each pair of nodes were joined by a spring whose rest length is the length of the shortest path between them. The trap is that igraph reads the weight column of the edges as a distance for this layout, whereas a similarity is the opposite of a distance: the most similar documents would be pushed apart, and the weakly tied ones drawn at the margins. With similarity weights, either use "fr" or ignore the weights with weights = NA.

ForceAtlas2

ForceAtlas2 ("forceatlas2") is the layout of the visualisation software Gephi, designed for the exploration of networks (Jacomy et al. 2014). Its forces are close to those of Fruchterman-Reingold, with two differences that matter for bibliographic networks. The repulsion between two nodes grows with the product of their degrees: with \deg_i the number of ties of node i and d_{ij} the distance between i and j,

F_{\text{repulsion}}(i, j) = k_r \, \frac{(\deg_i + 1)(\deg_j + 1)}{d_{ij}}, \qquad F_{\text{attraction}}(i, j) = w_{ij} \, d_{ij},

so that hubs, which have many ties, push other nodes away more strongly than peripheral nodes do. A gravity F_{\text{gravity}}(i) = k_g (\deg_i + 1) keeps the nodes around the centre. Finally, the speed of the nodes adapts to the stability of the system: it increases when forces are consistent and decreases when nodes oscillate.

set.seed(1)
laid_out_fa2 <- layout_networks(network, node_id = "source_id", layout = "forceatlas2")

The implementation of networkflow is compact: it computes the repulsion between all the pairs of nodes, instead of the approximation of Gephi, so that its cost grows with the square of the number of nodes. It is comfortable up to a few thousand nodes. Three arguments change the picture: scaling_ratio is the strength of the repulsion k_r (smaller values give a more compact layout), linlog = TRUE replaces the attraction by a logarithm of the distance, which separates clusters more, and strong_gravity = TRUE keeps disconnected components close to the centre.

UMAP

UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is not a graph layout: it is a method to embed points in a low-dimensional space while preserving their neighbourhoods (McInnes et al. 2018). It often gives nice visualisations, with compact and well separated clusters. It needs distances between points, which a network does not provide directly, so layout_networks() builds them from the network: the distance between two nodes is the length of the shortest path between them, an edge being as long as the inverse of its weight (a strong tie is a short one). UMAP then describes each node by its n_neighbors nearest nodes and finds coordinates that reproduce this neighbourhood structure.

set.seed(1)
laid_out_umap <- layout_networks(network, node_id = "source_id", layout = "umap", n_neighbors = 15)

n_neighbors is the size of the neighbourhood that is preserved: small values emphasise local structure and many small groups, large values a global view of the network. min_dist (0.1 by default) sets how tightly nodes are packed. The picture is thus partly built by the user, and a UMAP should be checked with several values of n_neighbors. Unlike force-directed layouts, UMAP does not put the nodes of two components close by default: nodes of different components are set farther apart than any connected pair. The package uwot computes it, and must be installed.

Comparing the layouts

The same network, with the same clusters, in three layouts, each node being coloured by its Leiden cluster (the labels are the cluster numbers).

network <- color_networks(network, column_to_color = "cluster_leiden", verbose = FALSE)
for (layout in c("fr", "forceatlas2", "umap")) {
  set.seed(1)
  laid_out <- layout_networks(network, node_id = "source_id", layout = layout)
  print(plot_networks(laid_out, cluster_label_column = "cluster_leiden", node_size_column = NULL))
}

None of them is the right one: they answer different questions.

Layout Idea Uses the weights Cost Reads well when
"fr" attraction along edges, repulsion between all nodes as attraction light a first look at a network of a few hundred nodes
"kk" geometric distances reproduce graph distances as distances (see above) grows fast with size small networks, unweighted or with weights = NA
"forceatlas2" as "fr", with a repulsion that grows with degrees as attraction square of the number of nodes networks with hubs, which need space
"umap" preserves the neighbourhood of each node through the shortest paths light networks of clusters one wants to see apart

A practical rule: try a force-directed layout first, and a UMAP to check whether the clusters found by Leiden also appear as separate groups of nodes. When a cluster is split or scattered in all the layouts, it is worth reading its documents again.

Colours and labels

color_networks() gives each cluster a colour, in the order of decreasing size of the clusters, and each edge a mix of the colours of its two ends. The colours are the ones of a palette that you can choose, here the perceptually uniform batlow palette of scico, and a category keeps its colour in every figure if the palette is given explicitly.

n_clusters <- length(unique(as_tibble(network, active = "nodes")$cluster_leiden))
palette <- data.frame(
  cluster_leiden = sort(unique(as_tibble(network, active = "nodes")$cluster_leiden)),
  color = scico::scico(n_clusters, palette = "batlow")
)
network <- color_networks(network, column_to_color = "cluster_leiden", color = palette, verbose = FALSE)

The label of each cluster is drawn at the centre of gravity of its nodes: prepare_label_networks() computes these positions, and plot_networks() calls it when they are missing. plot_networks() assembles the figure: edges as light arcs, nodes as points, the cluster labels, without decoration. It is meant as a quick, ready-made figure, and print_plot_code = TRUE prints the ggplot2 code, to copy and adapt for a figure to publish.

set.seed(1)
network <- layout_networks(network, node_id = "source_id", layout = "umap")
plot_networks(
  network,
  cluster_label_column = "cluster_label",
  node_size_column = NULL
)

For a list of networks (one per time window), layout_networks() accepts compute_dynamic_coordinates = TRUE, which starts the layout of each window from the positions of the previous one so that documents present in two windows stay in the same region: this is used in the last guide.

What comes next

A single network of the whole period mixes literatures that did not coexist. The last guide builds one network per time window and follows the clusters across windows.

References

Jacomy, Mathieu, Tommaso Venturini, Sebastien Heymann, and Mathieu Bastian. 2014. “ForceAtlas2, a Continuous Graph Layout Algorithm for Handy Network Visualization Designed for the Gephi Software.” PLoS ONE 9 (6): e98679. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0098679.
Kamada, Tomihisa, and Satoru Kawai. 1989. “An Algorithm for Drawing General Undirected Graphs.” Information Processing Letters 31 (1): 7–15. https://doi.org/10.1016/0020-0190(89)90102-6.
